lessons.focus: Vocabulary from Chapter 1

pre: Use Pre-lesson Task 12: Prepare jumbled-up words that make up a sentence about Akbar’s Dream (i.e. Akbar’s dream was to make the most beautiful silk cloth in the whole of India). The fastest group that can rearrange the words to make the sentence wins.
delivery: Divide pupils into groups. In groups, pupils read Chapter 1 of Akbar’s Dream together.
Pupils talk about the characters and the sequence of events.
Distribute the lyrics of the song from the guidebook (page 38) to each group.
Show the video clip http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nb3B5NZ6c-c to introduce the tune of the song to the pupils.
Pupils read the lyrics together and practise singing the lyrics with the tune.
Pupils perform the song in groups.
post: Use Post-lesson Task 1: Pupils listen to the actual song https://music.youtube.com/watch?v=5sxbWwauCDQ
Ask pupils to raise their hands up each time they hear something different from the lyrics they sang.

delivery: Follow the instructions for Activity 1 (Pupil’s Book, p.44) in the Teacher’s Book, pp.76– 77. Have pupils sit comfortably to read the story quietly on their own before talking about their global understanding of the story.

lessons.label: Writing 9
lessons.focus: Cohesion (e.g. but, because), punctuation, tenses review

pre: Choose a pre-lesson task from the list in Section 3 which reviews key areas of learning.
delivery: Using some examples of pupils’ mistakes in vocabulary or grammar, in particular use of cohesive devices (linking words) as well as punctuation, play a team game where you say a sentence with a mistake and pupils then write the sentence accurately, including punctuation.
Hand out the worksheet. Have pupils work first individually to try to correct the mistakes.
Ask pupils to compare their answers with their partner and discuss any differences. Then conduct feedback with the whole class.

Give some general feedback on pupils’ writing from Lesson 39. Remain positive to encourage pupils, focussing on the effort they made as much as the positive aspects of their writing. Focus specifically on the use of cohesive devices, as relevant.
Return pupils’ writing with your comments and markings on it. Explain the correction code if your pupils are not already familiar with it.

Have pupils work with a partner to correct the mistakes you have highlighted in their writing. It’s a good idea to have them do this in a different colour pen. Monitor and help pupils by guiding them with questions to make the corrections.
Collect pupils’ writing again. Briefly review their work and check the progress of pupils in their writing. You will use their work again in Lesson 48.
post: Choose a fun and active activity from the post-lesson tasks in Section 3 or refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book pp.14–17 for more ideas.

lessons.materials: Pupils’ writing from Lesson 39 with your feedback. Worksheet: Selection of sentences with mistakes from pupils’ writing, which pupils will correct together. Prioritise mistakes relating to the main and complementary learning standards. Note other examples of common mistakes to use as input in this lesson.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider monitoring carefully to support less proficient pupils. When you return their writing, make sure to speak to those whose writing is less good to encourage them and make sure they are not demotivated.

lessons.theme: World of Self, Family and Friends
lessons.focus: Present perfect review

pre: Choose an activity from the pre-lesson tasks in Section 3 or follow instructions for the Warm-up: What can we do? In Teacher’s Book, p.74.
delivery: Follow the instructions for Activity 1 in the Teacher’s Book, p.74. Pupils look at the job advert. Have pupils talk to a partner before feeding back as a whole class. Some of the vocabulary may be new to many pupils. Ask them to try to guess the meaning from the context of the job advert.
Follow the instructions for Activity 2 in the Teacher’s Book, p.74. Pupils look at the pictures to predict who is best suited to the job advertised in Activity 1.

Talk to pupils about the process of applying for a job, including the need for interview. Follow the instructions for Activity 3 in the Teacher’s Book, p.74. Pupils listen to the interview to find specific information about the interviewees.
Follow the instructions for Activity 4 in the Teacher’s Book, p.75. Have pupils discuss the questions in small groups of three or four.

Conduct feedback on groups’ discussions. Ask pupils whether their impressions of the people from the pictures were correct. Talk to pupils about the risks of pre-judging others based on appearance (CCE: Values).
Follow instructions for Cooler: Hiring a new teacher. If you have time, pupils could role play the interview in their small groups.
post: Review and consolidate learning in this lesson using a post-lesson task in Section 3 or refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book pp.14–17 for more ideas.

If you have extra time in this lesson, ask pupils to talk in pairs about a job they think their partner would be good at (CCE: Values).
post: Follow the instructions for Cooler: Come to my adventure camp in the Teacher’s Book, p.73.

lessons.label: Language Arts 9
lessons.focus: Sequencing adverbs: first, after that, next, finally

pre: Use Pre-lesson Task 5 (Sit down, Stand Up): Read statements that may be true or false from Chapter 1 of Akbar’s Dream. Pupils stand up if the statement is true and sit down if the statement is false (e.g. Akbar and his grandfather wanted to go to Agra to see the Taj Mahal - true)
delivery: Pupils read Chapter 2 of Akbar’s Dream (pages 12 - 21) together.
Get pupils to discuss and recall the sequence of events on Akbar’s journey to Agra without referring to their books.
Display jumbled up pictures of events and ask pupils to sequence them.
Divide pupils into groups and explain that they will be creating a booklet.
Distribute 4 sheets of A4 paper as well as pictures and excerpts from the guidebook (Appendices 1 and 2, pages 48 - 49) to each group.
Pupils cut each sheet into half, horizontally. Then, pupils cut out the pictures and excerpts to match them and arrange them in sequence.
Check pupils’ work before they paste the cut-outs onto the sheets of paper.
Pupils compile the sheets of paper to form a booklet and display their work in a gallery walk.
post: Use Post-lesson Task 8 (Test your memory): Have pupils review Chapter 2 for 1 minute. Hide one of the pictures of events and ask pupils to guess which picture is missing.

lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. If weaker pupils have difficulty, they could check their answers using the original text. You may also consider having less pictures and excerpts for weaker pupils for Steps 6.

lessons.label: Language Awareness 3
lessons.focus: Teacher to complete:

std.note: Language Awareness lessons should be presented and practised using a Main Skill and a Complementary Skill (Listening, Speaking, Reading or Writing). Teachers can use the Content and Learning Standards in the Year 6 DSKP.

pre: Review language from Unit 3 with an activity from the list of pre-lesson tasks in Section 3 or refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book pp.14–17 for more ideas.
delivery: Choose from activities from the Workbook Check-up Challenge pp.36–37, which reviews the language, vocabulary and skills covered in this unit. This choice should be based on your observations and notes on pupils’ progress and achievement in these units. Choose activities which will review areas pupils found challenging or which they may have forgotten. You could have pupils choose for themselves what they would like to do in this review lesson. See Teacher’s Book, p.75 for instructions and answer keys for activities.

Have pupils do a Listening task in pairs which is based on the Unit 3 theme. You could use practice test audio and material, or you could use audios or videos from the internet if you can’t find suitable listening material. Monitor as pupils do the listening activities and note their performance. Note: ● Plan any further activities for this unit to develop language skills according to your pupils’ needs. ● You can use information about your pupils’ performance which you collected using formative assessment strategies while teaching this unit. ● The information could include your observation of pupils interacting in classroom activities and their performance in written activities. ● Plan activities which focus on language practice in a meaningful, fun and communicative way.
post: Ask pupils to think about their learning and performance in this unit. They then complete the self-assessment worksheet. Pupils should do this in English (see below).
Collect the worksheets from pupils and review them to note pupils’ responses. If there are any areas of concern, prepare a review of these in upcoming lessons.

lessons.label: Reading 10
lessons.theme: World of Self, Family and Friends
lessons.focus: Present perfect with for (e.g. I’ve been a pilot for 12 years) and since (e.g. … since 2001)

pre: Play a dictionary race, where you give pupils words to race to find in the dictionary. Choose words from the texts in Pupil’s Book, pp.48-49 but not those in the box on page 48.
delivery: Follow the instructions for the Warm-up activity in the Teacher’s Book p.80. Pupils brainstorm and think about different jobs.

Tell the pupils the text title (Unusual Jobs) and show the pictures from the Pupil’s Book pp.48-49. Pupils tell their partner what they think the texts will be about. Ask pupils if they can think of other unusual jobs.

Explain to pupils that they will read one of the four texts in the Pupil’s Book. Pupils work in pairs. Give each pair a copy of one of the four texts. It is better to use copies than to have them use the book as they will read the other texts too. Ask pupils to read their text and find out which unusual job it talks about – they check their predictions from Step 3.

Write the words from the box in the Pupil’s Book, p.48 on the board. Ask pupils to look in their text and find one or more of the words. They should try to work out from the context what the words mean. Remind pupils they should think about how they worked out the meaning of the words.
Have pupils write a definition for their word(s) in their notebooks in pairs.

Hand out the dictionaries and ask pupils to find the word(s) and compare the dictionary definition with their own. They should check their understanding as they do this. If you don’t have access to enough dictionaries, pupils can refer to the Pupil’s Book, p.137, where the words are listed and defined.

Regroup pupils into groups of four to six so that there is at least one pupil with each text in each group. Pupils peer-teach the new words to their group and tell the group how they worked out the meaning of the word(s).
Pupils work either in their new group or in their previous pair. Follow instructions for Activity 3 in the Teacher’s Book, p.80. Pupils read all four texts to do the matching activity.
post: Play a game to review all the words from this lesson to check that pupils have understood their meanings from the peer teaching. You could choose a post-lesson task from Section 3, or you could refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book pp.14–17.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 48–49 Exercise(s): 2–3 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 80–81 Copies of the pictures from Pupil’s Book pp.48–49 Cut up copies of the four texts on Pupil’s Book pp.48–49 Dictionaries (optional)
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to note that different texts have more/fewer words from the box. Give more proficient pupils a text with more words to work with (Steps 4 and 5).

lessons.label: Writing 10
lessons.theme: World of Self, Family and Friends
lessons.focus: Present perfect with for (e.g. I’ve been a pilot for 12 years) and since (e.g. I’ve worked here since 2001)

pre: Review jobs vocabulary by asking pupils to tell the class some ‘cool jobs’. Have pupils justify their answers.
delivery: Follow the instructions for Learning to Learn in the Teacher’s Book, p.82, which focusses on skim reading skills.
Follow the instructions for Activity 1 in the Teacher’s Book p.82. Pupils practise skim reading to find the information to complete the table.

Using the worksheets, ask pupils to complete the gapped sentences. They can work in pairs or individually. These may be, for example: Adela is ____ pilot. Tyler _____ _____ a police officer for eight years. Jill chose her job _______ it is exciting and challenging. Derek enjoys _____ as a gardener.

pre: Review jobs vocabulary with a spelling game. Focus on jobs covered in the unit as well as jobs you think your pupils are interested in doing in the future. Leave the vocabulary written on the board.

Ask pupils to think about what they would like to do in the future. Have them write the job name in their notebooks (e.g. lawyer, doctor, cook). Monitor and help pupils with vocabulary as necessary and encourage them to use a dictionary to check the spelling if needed.
Based on the vocabulary on the board, have pupils write, in a column, three more jobs they’d quite like to do, in order of preference with the jobs they wrote in Step 3 at the top.

pre: Introduce pupils to the topic of codes by playing ‘Fizz-Bump’: Pupils stand in a circle (more than one circle if you have a large class) to play a counting game. In turns, going around the circle, they begin counting from 1. When a number can be divided by 3, pupils say fizz instead of the number; when divisible by 5, say bump. E.g.: (1) one – (2) two – (3) fizz – (4) four – (5) bump – (6) fizz (because 2x3=6) – (7) seven – (8) eight – (9) fizz (because 3x3=9) – (10) bump (because 2x5=10) and so on.
delivery: Reinforce the idea of codes by following the instructions for Cooler: Numbers and letters in the Teacher’s Book, p.95. Pupils should try to read words using a code. Note that this kind of code breaking supports pupils’ spelling.

post: Follow the instructions for Warm-up in the Teacher’s Book, p.94. Pupils write words beginning with the letters in their names.

pre: Review the topic of codes by having pupils work with a code (one from the previous lesson) to write sentences. The sentences should be a model of language for this lesson in negative and positive sentences, e.g. I think I will be a waiter when I grow up. / I don’t think I will be a footballer when I grow up.
delivery: Put the flashcards on the board and elicit the job vocabulary. Ask pupils to say what they would like to be when they grow up. Explain that sometimes we can’t do a job we’d really like when we are young (e.g. children who want to become professional sports or pop stars). Ask them, Do you think you will be a …? and elicit sentences similar to those in the warmer. Encourage them to say why/why not, using personality adjectives or other answers.

Have pupils write two or three sentences about what they think they want to be, what they will and won’t be when they grow up (e.g. I want to be a footballer, but I think I will be a sports teacher. I won’t be a doctor [because I don’t like blood!]). You may want to model this language specifically on the board before pupils begin writing.
Have pupils talk to their partner about their ideas from Step 3. They should explain their answers.
Elicit the process for a job application, starting with job advert, application, interview etc. Refer pupils back to the job advert in the Pupil’s Book, p.43.
Tell pupils they will see a job advert and should answer some MCQs (multiple-choice questions). Ask pupils to do the tasks on the worksheet individually first, then they can check with their partner.

Review the answers and ask pupils how they approached the task, e.g. read the job advert and highlight the key information; read the questions and answers; and eliminate the answers which are clearly wrong.
Ask pupils to imagine they have applied for this job. They talk to their partner: Will you get the job? Why? Why not?
post: Choose a post-lesson task from Section 3 to review and consolidate key learning, or you could refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book pp.14–17.

Follow the instructions for Activity 2 in the Teacher’s Book, p.102. Pupils fill in the gap.

pre: Gather pupils to the front of the classroom around you, or make sure they are sitting comfortably in their places. Tell the story you have chosen for this lesson. Make sure to include the beginning, middle and end. Ask a gist listening question to give pupils a reason to listen.
delivery: Ask pupils if they enjoyed listening to the story and give feedback on the gist question.

Tell pupils they will create their own stories in this lesson. Hand out the cut-up sentences from Pupil’s Book, p.67, one sentence per pupil. Note that these should be the first sentence given, not the questions and prompts, i.e. Tania sat up in bed. NOT She was excited because (Why?). Ask pupils to look at the picture and match their sentence to a picture.

Have pupils read the questions and prompts for their sentence on Pupil’s Book, p.67. In their notebooks, they write their sentence and then extend that stage of the story using the prompts given. They can answer these in any way they wish, even if it doesn’t exactly match the story.

Put pupils in groups of six so that the groups are made up of one pupil for each sentence/picture/stage of the story. Have pupils share their ideas to create a story. Note that the story may turn out oddly because it includes different ideas. Have pupils decide on a more logical progression of the story if necessary, although allow plenty of creativity and imagination – the story doesn’t have to be fixed.

Within the groups, pupils make pairs. In their notebooks, they work together to write the story. Allow plenty of time for this, and have pupils work together to co-write the story. Monitor and check pupils are participating equally.
post: Have volunteers read their stories to the class. The class should listen and identify any differences between what they hear and their own story.

lessons.label: Speaking 14
lessons.focus: Modal verbs for expression rules and obligation: have to, need to

pre: Review sports and activities vocabulary from the previous lesson using a task from the list in Section 3.
delivery: Show the picture of the skateboarder and ask pupils what kind of safety equipment the boy is using (helmet, knee and elbow pads). Teach the vocabulary using the picture. Explain that the boy needs use this to stay safe. However, he doesn’t have to use it – there are no rules to tell him to use this in skateboarding. Elicit more examples of need to and have to related to sports and activities. Write one or two examples of each on the board.

Put pupils into small groups. Tell them they will make a poster about safety in a sport or activity of their choice. Explain that pupils will need to decide for themselves how to approach and carry out the task. To do this, they should agree on the steps they need to take. First, have pupils assign different roles in the group (e.g. someone to write, to draw, to check vocabulary and spelling, maintain use of English and organise the project). Next pupils should decide a set of steps to complete the task (e.g. first, decide which sport or activity, then begin researching and designing our poster etc.) (CCE: Entrepreneurship).

Pupils make the posters in groups. Remind pupils that these are posters, not pictures, so they should put a little text on them which talks about the rules and what people need to do to keep safe. They should speak in English in their groups, however, and talk to each other to discuss the things people need or have to do for this sport. This will help prepare them to speak in the final stage of the lesson.
post: Conduct a gallery walk, where pupils walk around and look at each other’s posters. Have groups talk about their posters as you do this, in a casual way, focussing on rules and obligations.
Talk to pupils about the importance of following rules for fair play in sport (CCE: Values).

pre: Introduce the lesson with a fun, active pre-lesson task from the list in Section 3 which will review key vocabulary and ideas about video games.
delivery: Show the picture of the girl and tell pupils her name. Explain that she is ‘their’ email pen friend, and that she loves video games.

Handout the model email worksheet, which is an email from the girl to a pupil. In the email, she says that she loves playing and creating video game ideas. She writes about the steps of her favourite game (one she plays or has created) and recommends it. The email uses a range of target language from this lesson. Ask pupils to read the email, but first, set a gist question for them.
Draw attention to specific language used in the email, including both the target language and common expressions for opening and closing emails.

Explain that they are going to write a reply to the email. Hand out the next worksheet. It should give guidance on the worksheet about what to write in the email (e.g. – greet your penfriend and thank her for her email; – tell her if you like video games or not; – tell her the name of a video game you play; – tell her the main steps of this game; – finish your email), and how much to write (e.g. around 50 words).
Give pupils around 25 minutes to write their emails. Encourage them to do this individually, but monitor and help pupils as they work. Draw pupils’ attention to the model provided, as necessary.

Show pupils the evaluation criteria on the third worksheet and explain as necessary. Have pupils swap their papers with a partner and use the criteria to peer-evaluate. Make sure pupils provide constructive feedback by reminding them to make suggestions for improvement as well as to make a positive comment. Focus on this as a way to help their classmates learn better in a positive environment (CCE: Values).

If time, have pupils re-draft their emails based on the feedback, in another colour. If there is no time, you could ask pupils to do this for homework. Collect their work and use it for formative assessment.
post: Choose a post-lesson task from Section 3 to review and consolidate key learning, or you could refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book, pp.14–17.

lessons.focus: Suffixes (-tion; -sion); spelling of recently learned vocabulary

pre: Review the vocabulary and topic from the previous lesson with an activity from the pre- lesson tasks in Section 3. Focus on spelling as appropriate.
delivery: Remind pupils of the topic of the reading from the previous lesson and follow the instructions for Activity 2 in the Teacher’s Book, p.116, but have pupils try to answer the questions in pairs from memory before they read.
Follow the instructions for Working with words in the Teacher’s Book, p.116. Pupils work with -sion / -tion suffixes. Focus on pronunciation difference here (/-ʒən/ and /-ʃən/ respectively).
Play a word discrimination game: teacher says a word and pupils say if it ends with -sion or -tion. Repeat with a number of different words.
Hand out the worksheet. Have pupils choose one activity to do from the worksheet. First, they work on their own.
Pupils share their work with a partner to check together.
Have pupils look through the text again. They should find words which they think are difficult to spell (‘tricky words’). In pairs, pupils make a word game of their own using these words.
Pairs join another pair and complete each other’s word games.
post: Ask for volunteers to come to the front of the class and ‘deliver’ their word game. They may need to use the board for this, or project it on a screen if possible.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 70–72 Exercise(s): 2 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 116 Worksheet: Various spelling and word games (e.g. wordsearch, crossword, jumbled letters) using words from the text and/or recent lessons. Note: there are webpages that create wordsearches and crosswords, e.g. puzzlemaker.com.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider having fast finishers do a second activity from the worksheet in Step 5. Allowing choice of activity here will help motivate pupils. You could rank the activities from less to more difficult so pupils can choose their level of challenge too.

lessons.label: Listening 16
lessons.focus: Passive voice: Statements (e.g. be made from..)

pre: Follow the instructions for Warm-up: Tic-tac-toe in the Teacher’s Book, p.118.
delivery: Follow the instructions for Activity 1 in the Teacher’s Book, p.118. Pupils are introduced to the new target language.
Read aloud a section from the text in the Pupils’ Book, p.70–71. Have pupils listen and count how many passive forms you say.
Read it again and have them write the passive verb in their notebooks when they hear it.

Adapt Activity 2 in the Pupil’s Book, p.73 (see Worksheet in Materials/References column to the right). Hand out worksheets A and B to each pair of pupils, so that one pupil has A and one has B. In turns, pupils read aloud their sentence, pair by pair, while the partner listens. Together they decide which sentence in each pair sounds better.
Follow the instructions for Activity 3 in the Teacher’s Book, p.119. Pupils complete the text with the passive form.
post: Follow the instructions for Cooler: What are they made of? in the Teacher’s Book, p.119

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 73 Exercise(s): 1–3 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 118–119 Worksheet: Versions A and B. One of each pair of sentences from Pupil’s Book, p.73, Activity 2 on worksheets A and B each. Add more examples of pairs of sentences.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider using the video, if available, in Step 2 to engage pupils who prefer to watch this.

lessons.label: Speaking 16
lessons.focus: Passive voice: questions (e.g. What’s it made of?) and statements (e.g. It’s made of…)

pre: Follow the instructions for Warm-up: Telephone in the Teacher’s Book, p.120.
delivery: Introduce the items and materials using the realia. Use the passive voice when talking about what the items are made of, e.g. this clock is made of glass and metal.
Play a game to practise the new vocabulary. You could choose an activity from the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book, pp.14–17 or you could play a categorisation or brainstorming game/activity.
Follow the instructions for Activity 1 in the Teacher’s Book, p.120. Pupils hear the target language in context in the dialogue.
Follow instructions for Activity 2 in the Teacher’s Book, p.120. Pupils describe the objects.
Follow instructions for Activity 3 in the Teacher’s Book, p.120. Pupils make a new dialogue based on Activity 2.

Pupils work in groups. Give each group some realia. You could ask pupils to add to the realia using their own items. Pupils talk about the items they have, based on the model dialogue. Monitor and help with vocabulary. Also, check that all pupils are participating.
Give feedback by asking pupils to tell you what they have that is made of wood/metal/etc.
post: Play a guessing game where you describe items according to what they are made of and pupils guess what the items are, e.g. it is made of plastic, metal and glass. It is used for talking to people (answer: mobile phone).

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 74 Exercise(s):1–3 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 120 Realia (real things) of a range of common items found in the home made of different materials. You could ask pupils to bring some unusual items from home.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider asking each pupil to choose between two and five items to describe in Step 7. This would allow more proficient pupils to talk more, yet ensure less proficient or shy pupils also participate.

lessons.label: Language Arts 16
lessons.focus: Negative Imperative (Don’t)

pre: Show pupils a picture of a mother reprimanding her child.
Ask pupils to predict what the mother could possibly say.(See pre-lesson task 8)
delivery: Introduce the poem.
Pupils recite the poem in the intonation and voice of an adult.

Elicit responses from pupils:
• Why do parents set rules/are rules necessary?
• Have you ever felt angry when your parents tell you something?
• Do you like it when your parents forbid you from doing something you like?
Pupils give reasons for all ‘Don’ts’ in the poem. (Refer to activity on page 81 of the CCL guidebook)
Pupils work in groups. Every group brainstorms a list of things their parents have told them not to do.
post: Pupils set up a gallery walk. Pupils read all the “Don’ts” and put a sticker on every ‘Don’t’ their parents have said to them before.
Pupils compare the similarities and differences in the lists written by their friends and identify the most popular ‘Don’t’.

lessons.materials: Anthology of Poems for Year 4,5, and 6 Don’t by John Kitching Page 34 Contemporary Children’s Literature Teaching Guidebook (BPK) – Poetry
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils and class. Please see the seven differentiation strategies listed in the introduction. Please also consider the following: In addition, in Step 5, you may want to consider providing marker or model sentences for weaker pupils. This will increase their chances of success by being able to give responses.

lessons.label: Reading 17
lessons.focus: Passive voice: statements

pre: Introduce any new food vocabulary from the recipes for this lesson using a spelling activity from the list of pre-lesson tasks in Section 3.
delivery: Hand out the definitions worksheet. Pupils read the definitions and write the words. Pupils check in pairs before checking as a whole class. Remind pupils that they need to spell the answers correctly.
Show pupils the recipe on the second worksheet. Elicit the word ‘recipe’. Ask pupils if they enjoy cooking and whether they follow recipes to make food at home.
Have pupils read the two versions of the recipe and decide which one is correct. Pupils tell their partner why they think this.
Pupils re-read the correct recipe and underline the passive forms. Check answers in pairs before whole class.
Have pupils read the correct recipe again and mime it in pairs.

Tell pupils where you found the recipe (e.g. on the internet). Follow instructions for Learning to Learn in the Teacher’s Book, p.124. Talk to pupils about internet safety and how to identify real from fake information online (CCE: ICT; Values).
post: Ask for volunteers to come out and mime a recipe they know well. The class should guess what the pupil is making.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 77 Exercise(s): Learning to Learn Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 124 Worksheets: A writing task on definitions activity using passive voice, focussing on food e.g. Noodles are made of rice or wheat. Two versions of a recipe (using passive voice), one which is correct, the other with mistakes.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider adding in another activity to give more practice in the passive voice if your pupils are struggling with this form. This could come after Step 5.

lessons.label: Writing 17
lessons.focus: Passive voice (e.g. Water is added to…); linking words (Sequencing: first, second, next, then, finally)

pre: Use an activity from the list of Pre-lesson tasks in Section 3 to review the topic of food and introduce ‘pasta’.
delivery: Look through the activities on pp.76–77 and note any vocabulary which is new for pupils. Write the new vocabulary on the board. Give different pairs two or three words to check in the dictionary or in the word list at the back of the Pupil’s Book (p.137).
Hand out the worksheets. Ask pairs to find the definitions for their words from Step 2.

Have pupils mingle in order to find out which words their classmates think match which definition. They will need to talk about the words they worked with in Steps 2 and 3. They should not show their worksheet, but should communicate in English to find out what their classmates think.
Follow the instructions for Activity 1 in the Teacher’s Book, p.124. Pupils match the stages with the pictures in the infographic and complete the sentences using the passive voice.
Give feedback on the answers for Step 5. Introduce or review linking words for sequencing at this stage (see Look! box in Pupil’s Book, p.77), focussing on the use of commas where appropriate.
Follow the instructions for Activity 2 in the Teacher’s Book, p.124. Pupils answer questions to guide them in writing an introduction.
Follow the instructions for Activity 3 in the Teacher’s Book, p.124. Pupils work in pairs to write about how pasta is made. Remind them to use linking words to help the flow of their writing.
post: Review and consolidate new vocabulary and target language from this lesson with an activity from the post-lesson tasks in Section 3 or refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book, pp.14–17 for more ideas.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 76–77 Exercise(s): 1–3 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 124 Worksheet: Definitions for new vocabulary in this lesson. Dictionaries (optional)
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider nominating a few pupils to monitor in the mingling activity in Step 4 to remind pupils to speak English and not to show their worksheet to others.

lessons.label: Listening 17
lessons.focus: Review of passive voice

pre: Follow the instructions for Warm-up: What’s your favourite TV programme? in the Teacher’s Book, p.122.
delivery: Follow the instructions for Vocabulary in the Teacher’s Book, p.122. Pupils share their understanding of the words in the box in the Pupil’s Book, p.75.
Follow the instructions for Activity 1 in the Teacher’s Book, p.122. Pupils look at the pictures before listening and begin to think about the topic.
Follow the instructions for Activity 2 in the Teacher’s Book, p.122. Pupils listen to the adverts to decide what they are selling.
Follow the instructions for Activity 3 in the Teacher’s Book, p.123. Pupils identify fact and opinion (CCE: Values).

Follow the instructions for Activity 4 in the Teacher’s Book, p.123. Pupils listen again and answer questions about what they heard. Encourage pupils to try to answer the questions before they listen again.
Follow the instructions for Activity 5 in the Teacher’s Book, p.123. Pupils talk about which advert they like best.
post: Elicit some adverts that pupils like or know well. They may be on TV or another media. Have pupils talk about them in English.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 75 Exercise(s): 1–5 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 122–123
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider having pupils discuss their ideas in small groups in Step 8, as this will give more pupils the chance to speak in the time given. Some pupils may not like speaking to the whole class.

lessons.label: Speaking 17
lessons.focus: Use of language in advertising, e.g. great value; wonderful; only $XX

pre: Review the topic of recent lessons, focussing on the previous lesson in particular. You could use an activity from the list of pre-lesson tasks from Section 3.
delivery: Show the adverts. Pupils decide what each advert is selling. They talk to their partner and note their answer.

Play the recording of the adverts in Pupil’s Book, Lesson 5 (Audio 1.28, see Teacher’s Book, p.122). Discuss with pupils the kind of language strategies used to try to encourage people to buy the product. This may be using strong words like love or fantastic, or telling people it is free or just.. (CCE: Values; Financial Education)
Have pupils look again at the Pupil’s Book, p.75, Activity 2 to identify how language is used to sell the products.
Show the adverts you brought again. Have pupils identify similar language. If it is in their L1, have them try to translate it into English.

Tell pupils they will work in groups to create and perform an advert (CCE: Creativity & Innovation). Assign groups and hand out the worksheet. Pupils put the steps in order so that they can complete the task, e.g. – decide what you will sell in your advert; - decide what language you will use to encourage people to buy it; - write a script; - practise your advert; - perform your advert. (CCE: Values).
Read out the steps of the project in order. Pupils listen and check their answers from Step 6. Focus pupils’ attention further on the guidelines in the Pupil’s Book, p.78, Activities 3 and 4.
Pupils prepare their adverts. Monitor to offer support and encouragement. Make sure pupils practise their adverts.
post: Groups perform their adverts to the class. Have the class evaluate them in terms of the kind of language they use and how effective the adverts are in selling the product. Manage this stage so that pupils give constructive comments and plenty of praise. (CCE: Values). Make a note of some of the feedback points, so you can refer to it in Lesson 94.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 75, 78 Exercise(s): 3–4 Audio 1.28 (See Teacher’s Book, p.122) Three or four adverts from magazines and/or TV. These could be in English and/or L1. Worksheet: Jumbled sentences giving the steps of the mini project to follow.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, for Step 8, you may want to consider assigning one pupil per group to ensure everyone is on task and using English as appropriate.

lessons.label: Language Arts 17
lessons.focus: Negative Imperative (Don’t)

pre: Pupils share some ‘Don’ts’ that they remember from the poem (pre-lesson task 9: memory chain) before going through the poem.
Ask pupils instead of ‘don’ts’, what are some ‘do’s’ that their parents have told them before.
delivery: Pupils read the poem aloud using proper rhythm and intonation.
Tell pupils that they are now a poet.
Ask pupils to change the tone of the poem ‘Don’t’ into a positive tone by substituting the verbs or nouns. (Refer to CCL guidebook page 79).
post: Pupils recite their ‘Do’s’ poem to the class.

lessons.materials: Anthology of Poems for Year 4,5, and 6 Don’t by John Kitching Page 34 Contemporary Children’s Literature Teaching Guidebook (BPK) – Poetry
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, in Step 5, you may consider providing pupils with the verbs they need and have them match to the correct phrases. High proficiency pupils can come up with their own verbs or nouns or even change the phrases.

lessons.label: Reading 18
lessons.focus: Functional language: giving opinions (e.g. For me, it’s important that…)

pre: Follow the instructions in the Teacher’s Book, p.128 for Warm-up: Ready, set, draw.
delivery: Review the topic of jeans by asking pupils if they wear jeans. Encourage them to talk about the small differences between jeans they wear (or other clothes).

Tell pupils they will read about some jeans and answer some reading comprehension questions. Pupils do the activity on the worksheet on their own. Monitor and note how pupils do on this activity, and discuss the answers as a whole class.
Follow the instructions for Activity 1 in the Teacher’s Book, p.128. Pupils read the texts (including the one they have just read) and complete the table.
Tell pupils how many RM (Malaysian Ringgits) there are in £1 (pound). Show them how to convert £ into RM. Have them convert the prices shown in the texts. (CCE: Financial Education).
Follow the instructions for Activity 2 in the Teacher’s Book, p.128. Pupils talk about the different jeans.
Follow the instructions for Activity 3 in the Teacher’s Book, p.128. Pupils discuss how they would spend their £50. (CCE: Values).
post: Follow the instructions for Cooler: Football game, choose an activity from the post- lesson tasks in Section 3 or refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book, pp.14–17 for more ideas.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 79 Exercise(s): 1–3 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 128 Worksheet: Use one of the texts (Pupil’s Book. p.79) to create a reading comprehension assessment.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider having less proficient pupils work with just one or two of the texts in Step 4.

lessons.label: Writing 18
lessons.focus: Language and vocabulary review

pre: Choose an activity from the pre-lesson tasks in Section 3 to review key language and vocabulary that pupils continue to find challenging.
delivery: Show pupils the picture from the Workbook, p.70 (Activity 1). Ask pupils what they can see. Explain that it is a ketchup pen.
Hand out the worksheet. Pupils read the text and choose the best word(s) to fill the gaps. Pupils do this individually before checking in pairs.
Show the pictures of interesting inventions. Elicit some vocabulary for each picture, write these words on the board and put the picture next to the words.

Tell pupils they will write about an invention. This could be something they have invented themselves or it could be one of the inventions in the pictures. Have pupils write a first draft of their text, which can be modelled on the text from the Workbook.

Hand out the paper and ask pupils to draw their invention on the paper. Collect pupils’ writing and review it to identify common mistakes. Use a correction code to highlight mistakes in the target language. Have pupils’ work ready to return to them in Lesson 94.
post: Choose a fun activity to have pupils move around as they review language. Choose from the post-lesson tasks in Section 3 or refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book pp.14–17 for more ideas.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Workbook: Page: 70 Activity: 1 picture Worksheet: A reading task: MCQ gap-fill based on the text in the Workbook, p.70, Activity 1. Pictures of interesting inventions sourced from the internet. Paper for drawing.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider setting a minimum word limit for the writing task in Step 5.

lessons.label: Listening 18
lessons.focus: Use of language in advertising, e.g. No other XX is as useful as…

pre: Follow the instructions for Warm-up: Unscramble in the Teacher’s Book, p.126.
delivery: Follow the instructions for Vocabulary in the Teacher’s Book, p.126. Pupils are introduced to the new vocabulary.

Put the picture of the Lumina pen/torch on the board and ask pupils what it is. Write on the board the questions What’s it made of? and What can you use if for? and have pupils listen to Audio 1.29 from Pupil’s Book, p.78 and answer the questions.

Hand out the worksheet. Ask pupils to draw the product they heard about in Step 3 in the box on the right. Give just two minutes for this. Pupils then compare their picture with a partner. Show the picture in the Pupil’s Book, p.78, for pupils to compare their drawings with too.
Play the recording again. Pupils listen and complete the information on the left-hand side of the worksheet. Have them check in pairs before doing so as a class.

Write advantages and disadvantages on the board. Elicit the meaning of these words if they are new to pupils. Ask pupils to brainstorm in pairs the advantages (e.g. it’s small so you can fit it in your pocket) and disadvantages (e.g. it’s small so you can lose it easily) of the Lumina torch in their notebooks.
post: Lead a class discussion on the power of advertising and the media. Encourage pupils to think critically about the dangers and negative aspects of advertising and the media as well as the positive. (CCE: Values)

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 78 Exercise(s): 1–2 Audio 1.29 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 126 Worksheet: Copy the box in Activity 3, Pupil’s Book, p.78 onto a worksheet. Picture of Lumina pen/torch from p.78, Pupil’s Book.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider adding in some information onto the worksheet for Step 5 to reduce the amount pupils need to write, or have two versions of the worksheet, one requiring more writing of detail than the other.

lessons.label: Speaking 18
lessons.focus: Use of language in advertising, e.g. strong adjectives, e.g. wonderful, cool; giving advice to consumers, e.g. We think you should give it a try!

pre: Use some examples of pupils’ mistakes in their writing (from Lesson 92) in an error correction activity. You could conduct this as a game.
delivery: Remind pupils about the inventions they wrote about in Lesson 92 and the adverts they performed in Lesson 89. Explain that this lesson they will work on these ideas to create an advert for the radio.
Return pupils’ writing from Lesson 92, where they wrote about an invention. Have pupils work to correct the mistakes you have identified.
Review the key points of the peer feedback on pupils’ advert performances in Lesson 89.
Follow the instructions for Activity 3 in the Teacher’s Book, p.126. Pupils can use their invention from Lesson 92, their advert from Lesson 89 or another, new idea.

Follow the instructions for Activity 4 in the Teacher’s Book, p.126. In addition, have pupils include advice to certain groups of people (consumers/their ‘market’), e.g. All office workers should use this pen because… / We think you should try it! Pupils practice and perform their radio advert. This activity will allow them to improve on the previous oral advert they did in Lesson 89, based on feedback and on learning since then.
post: Follow the instructions for Cooler: Class survey in the Teacher’s Book, p.127.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 78 Exercise(s): 3–4 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 126–127
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider encouraging pupils to ask each other for help as well as asking you. in Step 3 in particular.

lessons.label: Language Arts 18
lessons.focus: First conditional, e.g. If you.., will..

pre: Write ‘Magic’ on board and elicit responses from pupils about what they know about magic.
delivery: Go through the features of the book cover with pupils.
Pupils brainstorm ideas (characters, setting, story) about the book.
Pupils name themselves with special names (e.g. Jason the Joker, Henry the Handyman, Dave the Deejay)
Pose a question “If you become a Wizard what would you do?” Pupils share their ideas.
Pupils describe the special powers they want to have and the reasons for having the powers.
post: Pupils imagine and design a costume for themselves as a witch or wizard.

lessons.materials: The Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum The Wizard of Oz Teacher’s Guidebook
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider encouraging pupils to ask each other for help as well as asking you in Step 5 and 6 in particular.

lessons.label: Language Awareness 5
lessons.focus: Teacher to complete:

std.note: Language Awareness lessons should be presented and practised using a Main Skill and a Complementary Skill (Listening, Speaking, Reading or Writing). Teachers can use the Content and Learning Standards in the Year 6 DSKP.

pre: Review language from Unit 6 with an activity from the list of pre-lesson tasks in Section 3 or refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book pp.14–17 for more ideas.
delivery: Choose from activities from the Review unit (Pupil’s Book pp.80–81, Activities 1–5), which review the language, vocabulary and skills covered in Units 5 and 6. This choice should be based on your observations and notes on pupils’ progress and achievement in these units. Choose activities which will review areas pupils found challenging or which they may have forgotten. You could have pupils choose for themselves what they would like to do in the review unit. See Teacher’s Book pp.130–131 for instructions for activities.

Have pupils do a reading task which is based on the unit theme. Collect their work and note their performance. Note: ● Plan any further activities for this unit to develop language skills according to your pupils’ needs. ● You can use information about your pupils’ performance which you collected using formative assessment strategies while teaching this unit. ● The information could include your observation of pupils interacting in classroom activities and their performance in written activities. ● Plan activities which focus on language practice in a meaningful, fun and communicative way.
post: Ask pupils to think about their learning and performance in this unit. They then complete the self-assessment worksheet. Pupils should do this in English (see below).
Collect the worksheets from pupils and review them to note pupils’ responses. If there are any areas of concern, prepare a review of these in upcoming lessons.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 80–81 Exercise(s): 1–5 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 130–131 Worksheet: A reading task. Self-assessment worksheet (see below).
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. Ask pupils to do the self-assessment in English. Monitor and give support to less proficient pupils as needed.

lessons.label: Reading 19
lessons.theme: World of Self, Family and Friends
lessons.focus: Future forms introduction: will, going to, present continuous

pre: Have pupils sit comfortably. Play the music extracts. Ask pupils how it makes them feel and whether they liked that music.
delivery: Follow the instructions for Activity 1 in the Teacher’s Book, p.132. Pupils are introduced to the names of different types of music and talk about music they like.

Follow the instructions for Activity 2 in the Teacher’s Book, p.132. Play the recording as pupils read the text. This will help their reading fluency and encourage them not to stop when they don’t understand something.
Follow the instructions for Activity 3 in the Teacher’s Book, p.133. Pupils guess the meaning of new words from context, then check them in the dictionary at the back of the book.
Ask pupils where the text (Pupil’s Book pp.82–83) comes from. Find out whether they read music magazines or read about music online.
Tell pupils they will hear a song in English and should decide what the topic of the song is. Write three options for this on the board, with one correct, the others incorrect.
Play the song. Pupils listen and decide what the song is about. They don’t need to understand every word of the song.
post: Use the song again in another activity. For example, pupils listen to the song again and stand up every time they hear a name or a particular word. You could have pupils sing along to the chorus, depending on the song you have chosen.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 82–83 Exercise(s): 1–3 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 132–133 Recordings of extracts of different types of music. Recording of a song in English which you think your pupils will know and which has clear lyrics.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider asking pupils to choose only three words from the box to guess and check in Step 4. More proficient pupils can check more. They can all then share their words with the class. This will save time.

lessons.label: Writing 19
lessons.focus: Adjectives to describe personality; prefixes: im- / un- / dis-

pre: Follow the instructions for Warm-up: One-question interview in the Teacher’s Book, p.132.
delivery: Follow the instructions for Activity 1 in the Teacher’s Book, p.134. Pupils review the reading text from the previous lesson and answer questions in Pupil’s Book, p.84.

Elicit and tell pupils more about the legend of Robin Hood, an English folk legend. Focus in particular on how he helped people and was a hero (CCE: Values). You could show a picture of Robin Hood or even an extract from one of many films about him.
Follow the instructions for Activity 2 in the Teacher’s Book, p.134. Pupils think about the focus and features of the two texts.
Follow the instructions for Working with words in the Teacher’s Book, p.134. Pupils look at modifying words in order to make them negative.
Ask pupils to highlight words which relate to personality. Brainstorm more adjectives to describe personality.
In pairs, have pupils use some of the words to describe Robin Hood. They discuss their ideas first.
Then, have pairs of pupils write at least four sentences to describe the personality of Robin Hood. Focus on the adjectives in particular and have pupils check spelling.
Pairs share and discuss their ideas with another pair to see if they agree.
post: Play a short extract from a Robin Hood film and ask pupils to check their personality adjectives. Or you could use the personality adjectives in a personalised activity, such as one from the list of post-lesson tasks in Section 3.

lessons.materials: Academy Stars Year 6 Pupil’s Book: Page(s): 82–84 Exercise(s): 1–2 Teacher’s Book: Page(s): 132, 134 Picture of Robin Hood and/or extract from a Robin Hood film.
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider the extension activity in the Teacher’s Book on p.135.

lessons.label: Listening 19
lessons.theme: World of Self, Family and Friends
lessons.focus: Present simple for future meaning

pre: Review the texts from the previous lesson by asking Questions 2 and 3 in Activity 3 in the Pupil’s Book, p.84. (CCE: Patriotism)
delivery: Ask pupils if they have ever been to or performed in a music concert to set the context of the dialogue.

lessons.label: Writing 21
lessons.theme: World of Self, Family and Friends
lessons.focus: Review of question forms (personal questions, e.g. What’s your favourite song to sing?)

pre: Using pupils’ recordings, play some songs at the beginning of the class. Ask pupils how each song makes them feel.
delivery: Elicit some information from the pupils about the singers or groups performing the songs played in Step 1. Make notes on the board, for example the names of the singer(s), the type of music, and so on.

Tell pupils they are going to interview a famous singer. In pairs, pupils should write between three and five questions to ask the singer. Remind pupils to use correct punctuation, in this case question marks in particular.

Pupils pass their questions to another pair. This pair should assume the role of the singer. They answer the questions in writing, but in note form (not full sentences). Encourage pupils to be creative at this stage in particular – their answers don’t need to be ‘real’. Or, if you have a lot of time and easy access to the internet, you could have pupils search for the actual answers the singer would give. They pass their answers back to the other pair.

Explain that pupils will write up the interview for a magazine or a blog. If you have a class blog or another publication, this would be a good place to ‘publish’ the interviews when they are finished.

Pupils look at their questions and the answers the other pair gave. They write up the interview for the magazine/blog. Set a minimum and maximum word limit. Monitor and help pupils, note areas of difficulty and common problems.
post: Give general feedback on their writing, making sure to give plenty of praise.

lessons.label: Speaking 21
lessons.theme: World of Self, Family and Friends
lessons.focus: Review of language (e.g. present simple for talking about themselves; past forms for narration)

pre: Choose an activity from the pre-lesson tasks in Section 3 above which suits the focus of your lesson.
delivery: Use this lesson to give all pupils the opportunity to practice a speaking assessment. Have pupils work in groups of three to conduct practice speaking tests, where there are two candidates and one examiner – one pupil plays the part of the examiner, using the examiner’s script. Pupils take turns to be the examiner so that each pupil has at least two practice speaking tests. Where possible, pupils could use different tests, but they can repeat the same if these are not available. Review any key language (e.g. expressions for checking understanding – see Pupil’s Book, p.30), which is part of ‘communicative competence’) and double check pupils know what is required in each part of the test. Pupils use a form to give each other feedback on their speaking and to self-assess each time they are a candidate. The criteria on the form should be simple and should focus on the speaking assessment criteria, e.g. the use and accuracy of grammar; the use and accuracy of vocabulary; communicative competence. Avoid asking pupils to score each other; instead, they could say if it was: great / good / ok / needs work. Encourage comments if appropriate. Talk to the pupils about these assessment criteria so that they understand what they mean. Collect the assessment forms to review them as formative assessment evidence.
post: Give whole class general feedback. Give tips as necessary and remind pupils that they will be with their friends in the exam, and just need to talk about themselves, so there is no need to feel nervous.

std.note: Language Awareness lessons should be presented and practised using a Main Skill and a Complementary Skill (Listening, Speaking, Reading or Writing). Teachers can use the Content and Learning Standards in the Year 6 DSKP.

pre: Review language from Unit 7 with an activity from the list of Pre-lesson tasks in Section 3 or refer to the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book p.14-17 for more ideas.

lessons.label: Speaking 23
lessons.theme: World of Self, Family and Friends
lessons.focus: 1 st conditional if clauses (If + present, will / might / may / could + vb: e.g. If I go to Japan, I might visit…)

pre: Choose a pre-lesson task from the list in Section 3 above to review key language (if clauses).
delivery: Use the pictures from the topic cards to introduce each topic and have pupils brainstorm words related to each topic in small groups.

Pupils work in groups of about six. They sit in a circle. Each group has one set of cards. A pupil takes a card and makes a future prediction about that topic using a modal verb (e.g. holidays: We might go to Japan in the holidays; environment: the rainforest might disappear in the future.) They pass the card to the pupil on their right, who also makes a sentence. Each sentence should be different, as far as possible. This pupil passes the card and so on. Repeat for all cards.

Have pupils work in pairs in the groups of six. Pupil A takes a topic card and makes a prediction using the card (these can be similar to previous ones if they have run out of ideas); pupil B then makes an if clause, e.g. Pupil A: We might go to Japan in the holidays. Pupil B: If you go to Japan in the holidays, you could visit the temples in Kyoto. They exchange roles for the next card and continue until they have used all the cards.
In pairs, pupils choose a topic. They write sentences using the target language in their notebooks.
Give feedback by asking pupils to read their favourite sentences to the class. Ask the class to decide which one is most original
post: Choose an activity from the post-lesson tasks in Section 3 or an activity from the Games Bank in the Teacher’s Book, pp.14–17 to review key learning in the lesson.

lessons.label: Speaking 26
lessons.theme: World of Self, Family and Friends
lessons.focus: Functional language: giving opinion (e.g. I don’t believe that…), checking understanding, e.g. using reported speech (e.g. You said ….., didn’t you?)

pre: Review the names of topics which have been covered in this unit (Multi-tasking; School uniforms; Advertising; Healthy eating) with a word game from the pre-lesson tasks in Section 3.
delivery: Tell pupils they will have a debate in groups. Explain that in a debate, there is a ‘motion’ – this is a statement, which gives an opinion on a topic (see A–D below). One side agrees with the motion (For), the other side disagrees (Against). Hand out the worksheet and point out the three motions: A - Multi-tasking is the best way to work. (CCE: Values) B – Children are happier at school when they wear a uniform. (CCE: Values) C – Advertising helps people make the best choices for healthy eating. (CCE: Values) D – Children need sugar to give them energy (CCE: Values)

Pupils work in groups of four. Each group first decides on a motion to debate. Then, on the worksheet, they discuss the ideas both for and against the motion they have chosen. Each pupil should make notes on the worksheet.

Assign For and Against roles to pairs of pupils in each group. As with a real debate, their position may not be the same as their own opinion. Have pupils prepare their arguments and practise what they will say.

Explain that there will be three stages to the debate: Stage 1- the For side gives their opinion while the Against side listens and take notes. Stage 2 – the Against side gives their opinion while the For side listens and takes notes. Stage 3 – there is an open discussion, where pupils use their notes to check understanding of what was said and to expand their opinions according to their For or Against role (e.g. You said ….., didn’t you, but we disagree. We believe that…). Pupils will need to use reported speech and expressions for checking understanding of the speakers for this stage of the debate. Remind pupils of the Value (Listening to and respecting each other’s opinions: CCE). Monitor carefully as pupils work on this activity to make sure they are co-operating with each other and the debate is running smoothly in each group.
post: Give feedback on the content of the different debates as well as on language used, especially relating to the target language.

lessons.materials: Worksheet: A table with the four blank rows (one for each motion) and two blank columns (one for For and one for Against notes).
lessons.differentiation: Differentiate learning according to the needs of your pupils. Please see the seven differentiation strategies in Section 4. In addition, you may want to consider reviewing key language and expressions for Stage 3 of the debate before pupils begin Step 5. Write these on the board for pupils to refer to as they need them. Consider using contribution cards (e.g. each pupil has 5 cards to ‘use’ when they say something in the debate) to support less proficient or shyer pupils in their participation.

delivery: Write the title of the text: The Power of Stories on the board. Ask pupils to think and share what the text will talk about.

Give each pupil a copy of the first paragraph of the whole text (i.e. from Stories are an important part… to …how did it all begin?.). Have pupils answer the first question in the text in small groups: Do you remember…?

Explain that different groups of pupils will have different sections of the text on pages 118–120 of the Pupil’s Book. Pupils read their text and answer the question.

Ask pupils to look at Activity 1 in the Pupil’s Book, p.121. They should find at least one description that relates to their text and match it to the stories. Pupils can check their answers with others in the same large group.
In a similar way, have pupils identify and answer the questions in Activity 2 in the Pupil’s Book, p.121 which they can answer based on their text.

In these groups of three, pupils discuss the questions in Activity 4, Pupil’s Book, p.121.
post: Talk with the class about the value and importance of reading. Ask pupils about their reading habits and encourage them to read as often as they can, in English as well as in their own language.

pre: Ask pupils about stories they know from other cultures.
delivery: Review the text from Lesson 139 by asking pupils to share what they remember about different stories.

Tell pupils they will work with some stories from other cultures. Hand out the worksheet. Pupils look at the pictures and match them to the titles of the stories. There is no need to check answers at this stage.
Next, ask pupils to match the sentences to the right story. Don’t check answers at this stage.
Play the stories, one by one. After each story, stop and check pupils’ answers on their worksheets.

Ask pupils to discuss the questions on the worksheet in pairs or groups of three:
• Do you know any of these stories already? Which ones?
• Where do you think these stories come from? Why?
• Which story do you like best? Why?
• Which story has the strongest moral message? What is it?
Give feedback on their answers and discuss the questions as a class.

Ask pupils to choose one of the stories. They can choose a task, A or B, and should decide on the steps to complete the tasks by themselves. They make a note of the steps they decide. Check these as a class. (CCE: Values – cooperation and team work). Task A: Make a poster. The poster should be illustrated. Pupils should write their opinion of the story, supporting their ideas carefully. Pupils should be ready to present their posters in the next lesson. Task B: Perform a scene. Pupils choose a scene from the story and act it out. They should write and try to learn the script. Pupils should be ready to present their scene in the next lesson.
post: Play a mime game, where you mime a scene from one of the stories. Pupils should guess which story it is or which character you are. Have pupils mime to the class too.

lessons.materials: Three or four short stories (spoken) from different cultures (e.g. stories from around the world on YouTube). Worksheet: Pictures from the stories and titles, for matching.
